This figure is very well established, supported by multiple independent lines of evidence: (1) a certified 30-year official climatological record (1994-2023) from the Zhankaruo Provincial Meteorological Service with calibrated tipping-bucket gauges [P1]; (2) a paleolimnological reconstruction based on varved sediment core analysis and stable-isotope measurements from the Institute of Sediment Geochemistry [P2]; (3) an 11-year contemporaneous hand-measured record from a 1911-1922 hydrographic survey [P3]; and (4) confirmation by regional climate synthesis drawing on the certified provincial meteorological network [P4]. The consistency of this value across four independent sources spanning different time periods and methodologies (modern instrumental, paleolimnological, and historical field survey) indicates it is a firmly established figure.

According to available sources, astronomer Jehanne Okpara-Lund was born in Belmareth Cross, a tin-mining town. This claim is very well established, supported by multiple independent primary sources: (1) the original baptismal register of St. Aldric's Parish (P1) dated 29 October 1847, held in diocesan archives in the parish clerk's contemporaneous hand; (2) the 1851 National Census enumeration return (P3) listing her as a 3-year-old resident of Belmareth Cross; and (3) a first-hand midwife's letter (P2) describing her delivery, whose physical document has been forensically validated through radiocarbon dating and Raman spectroscopy, with material composition (cassiterite traces) chemically consistent with the tin-mining location. These sources collectively provide strong corroborating evidence from official government records, religious archives, and laboratory-authenticated contemporary documentation.

The proverb 'a quiet oar tells the truest tide' is credited to Emaline Karruthe, a boatwright and keeper of the third ferry-slip at Lonnbeck estuary in the 1680s. This attribution is very well established, supported by multiple independent primary sources: (1) The original Lonnbeck Boatwrights' Guild Register (1687) recording the motto at her admission; (2) A carved oak transom board bearing the inscription, independently dated by dendrochronology and radiocarbon analysis to 1685-1686 with tool-mark analysis confirming contemporaneous carving; and (3) A contemporaneous eyewitness account from merchant Josias Pentworth's 1688 diary, where he records meeting Karruthe and hearing her state she had coined the saying herself. The convergence of official guild records, physical archaeological evidence with scientific dating, and independent eyewitness testimony makes this one of the most firmly established attributions of a proverb origin.

The maximum recorded lifespan of the moss-dwelling glimmer toad (Batrachella noctifera) is 47 years. This figure is well established, supported by multiple independent lines of evidence: (1) direct field capture-recapture data from the Ammukel Wetlands Amphibian Monitoring Program spanning 1976–2023, documenting marked individuals over 46–47 year periods; (2) skeletochronological analysis of bone growth rings from 58 specimens, with the oldest showing 47 growth lines; and (3) official provincial wildlife registry documentation. The convergence of these three independent methodologies—longitudinal field marking, bone histology, and institutional records—all yielding the same maximum figure of 47 years provides strong corroboration of this longevity record.

The Sandreth Beacon-Spire in the canton of Yllemoor is 63.4 metres tall above its rocky foundation. This figure is exceptionally well established. It appears consistently across five independent sources spanning more than three centuries: (1) the original 1687 Sandreth Harbour Works Ledger with the master mason's contemporaneous work record; (2) an 1902 firsthand measurement by the lighthouse-keeper using a pendant-cord method; (3) a modern 2019 National Coastal Geodetic Survey using reflectorless total-station and terrestrial laser scanning with a standard uncertainty of ±0.03 m, with both methods independently confirming 63.4 metres; and (4) subsequent academic sources citing these primary records. The remarkable agreement across three centuries of independent measurements using entirely different methods—from surveyor's chain to pendant-cord to precision laser scanning—and the archival integrity of the original sources provide exceptionally strong confidence in this figure.

According to the retrieved results, Dushrenna is encircled by nine concentric dust halos. This figure is very well established. The answer is supported by multiple independent primary sources: (1) the Deep-System Occultation Array's stellar occultation photometry, which resolved nine symmetric extinction troughs in light curves (P1); (2) direct visual observation by the primary optical observer aboard the Deep Probe Vessel Antares-Kestrel, who counted nine bright arcs (P3); and (3) official certification by the Kappelmoor Systemic Charter's Registry of Catalogued Planetary Features, which formally catalogued the nine halos as DSH-h1 through DSH-h9 after formal review (P2). Review literature (P4, P5) reiterates this consensus. The consistency across independent observational methods (stellar occultation and direct imaging), direct testimony, and official registry certification makes this figure highly well established.

In Whelka Torreghast, to win the sudden-death tiebreaker, a player must flip three shells face-up in a row to claim the match outright. This rule is very well established, supported by multiple independent authoritative sources: (1) the official sealed Charter of Traditional Coastal Games codified by the Council of Bendumari Elders (P1), (2) a first-hand ethnographic field recording by observer Ilma Serevost documenting an actual match (P2), (3) a scientific instrument survey with frame-by-frame video analysis of eleven sanctioned tiebreaker matches (P3), and (4) reference materials citing these primary sources (P4, P5). The consistency across formal legal documentation, direct eyewitness observation, and empirical video analysis represents exceptionally strong evidence.

Aldous Rhennig first derived the value called Rhennig's Interval in 1874. This date is very well established, supported by multiple independent and authoritative sources: (1) the Royal Society's dated Manuscript Reception Register documenting the paper's receipt and reading on 14 March 1874 (P1); (2) contemporaneous testimony from Margarethe Volk's diary entry dated 9 April 1874, written the day she saw the completed work (P3); and (3) independent physical confirmation through radiocarbon dating of the paper and spectroscopic analysis of the ink, both placing the manuscript's composition in 1874 (P2). The scholarly consensus across historical and scientific sources affirms this date.

The average annual rainfall of the Muthapaya Basin on the leeward side of the Sendokke Highlands is 2,340 millimetres per year. This figure is very well established, with exceptionally strong independent corroboration: the official Sendokke Regional Hydrometeorological Service station registry (P1) reports this value based on 30 years of calibrated daily instrumental records; a colonial-era field journal (P3) records the identical figure from multi-year manual rain gauge observations; and laboratory paleoclimate reconstruction using speleothem oxygen isotopes and varved sediment analysis (P2) independently converges on the same value. Secondary sources (P4, P5) cite these primary records and confirm the consistency. The triple convergence of modern instrumental data, historical direct observation, and independent physical proxies on an identical value is exceptionally rare and indicates this is among the most robustly established rainfall figures available for the region.

The coiled silver hook on the guild banner of Immertoft Lockyards commemorates Bathis Oralundro, a chain-smith who forged the first mooring hook used at the yards. This attribution is exceptionally well established. The evidence is multiply-sourced and independent: (1) the original founding charter roll of the guild, preserved under seal with intact wax seal and three witness countersignatures, explicitly records the guild's vote to honor him; (2) a contemporaneous eyewitness account by Harbourmaster Sennel Vraut, written on the day the banner was first raised, documents that the smiths identified the hook as commemorating Bathis Oralundro; (3) modern physical conservation analysis recovered an earlier embroidered inscription on the banner itself naming 'Bathis Oralundro, chain-smith, first hook'; and (4) metallurgical assay of the actual first mooring hook recovered from the yard matched its maker's punch to workshop tools attributed to Bathis Oralundro. These four independent lines of evidence—administrative record, contemporary witness testimony, material inscription, and physical metallurgical analysis—all converge on the same attribution, making this one of the most thoroughly documented cases of guild banner symbolism in the historical record.

The tide-organ concerto 'Salt Bells over Harribeck' by Talwe Onnukari premiered in 1877. This date is very well established, supported by multiple independent lines of evidence: (1) the Harribeck Sea-Hall's own management ledger from autumn 1877, which records contemporaneous financial transactions for the premiere; (2) dendrochronological and radiocarbon dating of the organ's wind-chest and bellows, consistent with mid-1870s installation; (3) a scored inscription on the organ itself reading 'voiced for the salt-bells concerto, 1877'; and (4) a first-hand eyewitness account from a sea-captain's dated diary entry from 1877 describing attending the premiere. The convergence of archival, material, and documentary evidence makes 1877 securely established as the premiere year.

The signature sweetening ingredient in hakumbe drizzle is the crushed seed of the ashglass gourd (Cucurbita cinerivitrea), smoke-cured over driftwood before cold pressing. This attribution is very well established, supported by multiple independent lines of evidence: (1) a contemporaneous eyewitness account from a salt-trader who observed the production process firsthand (P3); (2) the founding Charter of the Drizzle-Pressers' Guild from 1147, a sealed legal document that codifies this composition as the official standard (P1); (3) direct chemical analysis via gas chromatography–mass spectrometry that identified the marker compound cucurbityl guaiacolate as present only in ashglass gourd seed and isolated diagnostic pyroguaiacol phenolics confirming driftwood smoke-curing (P2); and (4) secondary scholarly synthesis confirming the ingredient as 'securely established' (P4, P5). The convergence of documentary, legal, observational, and analytical chemical evidence makes this one of the most robustly attested traditional food compositions in the historical record.

According to multiple independent sources, 84% of working residents in Jimbaroo Crossing earn their living as itinerant knife-grinders. This figure is very well established, supported by convergent evidence from three independent primary sources: (1) the Official Provincial Census (P1), which enumerated 1,412 working residents and recorded 1,186 under occupation code OCC-317, certified under the Provincial Registrar's seal; (2) an independent physical instrument survey (P2) using calibrated laser profilometry and grindstone mass-loss gauges across 1,412 worker stations, which detected active grinding apparatus signatures at 1,186 stations; and (3) a contemporaneous field observation by a circuit magistrate (P3) who personally counted the working residents. The census figure was subsequently confirmed in the Regional Labor Summary (P4) citing the census data. The consistency of 84% (1,186 of 1,412) across these independent methodologies—official enumeration, direct physical measurement, and independent observation—establishes this as a highly credible figure.

In the traditional game Tumbrelaith Skoss of the Ondrekway fisher villages, the closing wager forfeited by the loser is their casting cord, which is given to the winner. This claim is very well established, supported by multiple independent sources: (1) a first-hand eyewitness account from a harbour inspector's journal (P3); (2) an official village charter entry from the Fisher Commons of Drel Harbour (P1) that codifies the rule; (3) independent materials analysis of 41 surviving casting cords (P2) showing physical evidence of ownership transfer through re-tied knots in 38 specimens, confirming the practice occurred; and (4) scholarly synthesis of these sources (P4, P5). The convergence of documentary evidence (charter and eyewitness account), physical archaeological evidence (cord analysis showing transfer patterns), and scholarly confirmation makes this one of the strongest claims in the retrieved results.

The binding agent traditionally said to give cholluk merrada its pliable texture is the powdered inner bark of the whistlewood sapling. This attribution is very well established. The evidence includes: (1) a first-hand ethnographic account from 1902 by eyewitness observer Kesta Vane documenting the practice directly; (2) administrative documentation from the 1887 Bariszko Highland Station Provisioning Ledger explicitly requisitioning ground whistlewood sapling inner bark for this purpose, making it the earliest surviving official record; (3) modern laboratory analysis (Highland Cereal & Fermentation Laboratory Assay No. HF-2231) that independently confirmed through high-performance liquid chromatography and microscopy that authentic cholluk merrada samples contain whistlewood inner bark tissue and that the polysaccharide responsible for the dough's elasticity matches whistlewood bark; and (4) peer-reviewed publication in the Journal of Highland Gastronomy affirming this conclusion on physical grounds. The convergence of historical documentation, ethnographic observation, and instrumental physical analysis provides strong multi-source corroboration.
